angles.title: The starter is the whole bakery
angles.thesis: The bread part is really about patience with the slow invisible part of the work, the part that happens before anyone sees anything.
angles.audience: newsletter readers; the memo calls it the best story the writer has heard in months but names no narrower reader

uses.quote: the first month they are not allowed to shape a single loaf
the starter is the whole bakery
the failure happened twelve hours before they touched the dough
the patience of reading back through your own records instead of guessing
Not his shaping, not his scoring, the fact that he noticed the starter.
the slow invisible part of the work, the part that happens before anyone sees anything

open_questions: Is the piece about patience with invisible work, or about keeping records and reading them back (the notebooks)? The memo raises both.

angles.title: The agenda is upside down
angles.thesis: The weekly meeting should be for decisions and disagreements only, with status updates moved into a short written document.
angles.audience: the writer's own team and its managers

uses.quote: half the agenda is status updates that could be a written document
we spent seventy minutes on updates and twenty minutes on the one decision that actually mattered
The thing that needs the whole room gets the least time.
the Monday meeting is only for decisions and disagreements. If there is no decision on the agenda, we cancel the meeting.
each update is three lines, what changed, what is blocked, what decision you need
the meeting facilitator should change every week

open_questions: Is this a proposal to the team, or an essay for a wider audience about meetings? The memo says the team needs it.
How should the piece answer the managers, who 'will hate that, because the meeting is where they feel informed'?

angles.title: Write the toolbox, not the thesis
angles.thesis: The small specific thing is the only way a reader gets in, so start with one object or one person and let the big idea show up on its own.
angles.audience: people who write in public, and the writer's own newsletter readers

uses.quote: I keep stalling because every draft feels too small
I have a feeling, not an argument.
Nobody wrote back to the big abstract ones. So why do I keep starting with the abstract?
But the small specific thing is the only way a reader gets in.
Write the toolbox, not the thesis.

open_questions: Does this need its own concrete object to practise what it preaches? The toolbox and parking-garage essays are already published pieces.

angles.title: The small invisible daily thing

uses.quote: The small invisible daily thing, the starter, the notebook, the toolbox. Maybe that is the actual essay. I don't know yet.
Is it one piece or three pieces? I genuinely can't tell.
the slow invisible part of the work
the small specific thing is the only way a reader gets in

open_questions: What does the combined piece argue? The memo names a connection (starter, notebook, toolbox) but no claim.
Does the meeting material belong? The memo's own list of connections does not mention it.
One piece or three? The writer says they can't tell yet.

audience.value: Team leads who reward visible output over slow groundwork.

purpose.value: Team leads should come away seeing that they judge people at the oven when the work is decided at the starter, and should go find whoever on their team quietly tends the groundwork and start crediting it as real output.

evidence.quote: I have been trying to write in public for about two years, short essays, mostly on a newsletter

length.skipped: Writer doesn't want to commit to a length yet.

thesis.value: The slow invisible part of the work decides the result, long before anyone sees it.

value: The first month: new bakers may not shape a single loaf; they feed the starter, clean baskets, log the cold-room temperature (line 3)
The starter is the whole bakery: the failure happened twelve hours before they touched the dough; you cannot rescue bad fermentation with good scoring (line 5)
The notebooks: eleven years of batch records, read back instead of guessing (line 7) - first to cut if long
The baker who noticed the dough rising slower on rainy days - the turning scene (line 9)
The Monday team meeting material (memo lines 13-21)
